newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia, Indonesia sign maritime treaty.
newsitem.headline: Australia, Indonesia sign maritime treaty.

text.p: Australia and Indonesia on Friday signed a historic sea boundary treaty after some 30 years of negotiations, establishing exclusive economic zones between the two Asia-Pacific nations.
"Once it enters into force, the treaty will be of economic benefit to both countries," Australian and Indonesian foreign ministers said in a joint statement after signing the treaty.
"The finalisation of the seabed boundary provides a basis on which exploitation of natural resources can proceed in a climate of confidence and certainty," they said.

The sea boundary is 3,000 kms (1,840 miles) long, but does not affect the 1989 Timor Gap Treaty which covers exploitation mainly of oil and gas reserves in the Timor Sea between Timor island and Australia.
The Timor Gap Treaty went into effect in 1991 and has a lifespan of 40 years.
The sea boundary treaty is the first major bilateral international treaty to be signed by Australia's conservative government since it came to power in March last year.
"It's fair, it's equitable, it's in Australia's national interests," said Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said the treaty reflected a strong bilateral relationship, despite past spats over trade and human rights.
"There have occurred many events that in one way or another have caused tension in the relations between our two countries," Alatas told reporters.

"Yet our relations remain broadly...stable because of the very same spirit of mutual respect and partnership which motivated our two countries to assiduously negotiate these maritime boundaries issues," he said.
